5. RISC-V

5.1. Introduction

An Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) is a standard that defines how software interfaces with hardware. For example, it specifies

  • Low level instructions
    1. Syntax, e.g. ADD R1, R2, R3
    2. Encoding (how that instruction is represented in bits.) , e.g. maybe some bit pattern means opcode = add, destination = R1, sources = R2 and R3.
    3. Semantics (what the instruction does), e.g. addition
  • Fundamental architecture features and design

Different CPUs implement different ISAs:

  • x86 (1978, CISC): Intel i9, i7, i5, i3, and many AMD processors
  • ARM (1981, RISC): Used in many cell phones and the basis for Apple silicon (Apple has its own version)
  • MIPS (depracated in favor of RISC-V)
  • RISC-V (2010, open source)

In 1970s and 1980s, complex instruction sets could reduce size and memory accesses of programs at the exchange of being expensive to design and implement. These are called Complex Instruction Set Computers (CISC).

Reduced instruction set computers (RISC) keeps the instruction set small and simple, and pushes complexity into the software and compiler. Much easier to build faster hardware.

5.2. Processors, Registers, and Memory

Conceptual layout of a computer is shown below (von Neumann architecture):

  • Processor (CPU) is responsible for computing via a control unit and a data path. The latter contains registers and an arithmetic logic unit.
  • Memory (RAM)
  • I/O devices (e.g. keyboards, display, disk)
  • If processor runs at 4 GHz, then it needs to be able to execute an instruction once every 0.25ns. Accessing something 10cm away will take 0.3 ns based on the speed of light.
  • Registers have limited space and are lightning fast, and a processor performs operation on these data using the ALU.
  • Memory access is located external to the processor and often assumed to take approximately 100 ns.
  • Each ISA specifies a predetermined number of hardware registers. RISC-V defines 32 registers each with 4 bytes.
  • Comparison: While a processor has only about 32⋅4=128 bytes of total register storage, a laptop might have 2 to 64 gigabytes of DRAM, and a server might have a terabyte. On the other hand, if we think in terms of latency, registers are about 50 to 500 times faster than DRAM. The main bottleneck is not distance but the complexity of the circuit

5.3. RISC-V ISA

  • Recall ISA specifies both assembly language and machine language (bit level).

    • An assembly instruction has an operation name (opname) and operands that specify source and destination registers, values, memory locations, other instructions, etc.
    • For example, add x1 x2 x3 adds the values of registers x2 and x3 and stores it in x1. This becomes 32 bits o f machine code.

  • There are no variable names in assembly. Assembly instructions use register numbrs or names. They are numbered x0 to x31 and have names specified by the ISA. E.g. x0 has name zero.
